messages.content: I keep building API URLs by gluing strings together, like base + "/search?q=" + term. It works until it doesn't. What actually goes wrong?

String splicing treats the URL as plain text, but a URL is a structured format with escaping rules, and user data routinely contains characters that are structural in that format.

Concrete failures:

- A search term like `fish & chips` splices into `?q=fish & chips` — the server sees two parameters, `q=fish ` and a stray ` chips`, because `&` is the parameter separator.
- A term with `#` truncates everything after it (fragment), a term with `+` or `%` gets decoded into something you never sent, and a value with a space or non-ASCII characters may be rejected or mangled depending on the server.
- A value that itself contains `=` or `&` lets caller data inject extra parameters — the query-string equivalent of SQL injection.

The fix is to never put raw data into a URL string. Build the query with `urllib.parse.urlencode`, which percent-encodes each key and value according to the rules, and let it assemble the separators. The general principle travels: whenever you embed data into a structured format — URLs, JSON, SQL, HTML, shell — use the encoder/builder for that format instead of concatenation. Concatenation is how injection bugs are born.
Show me the right way to build a search URL with several parameters, including a tag filter that repeats the same key twice.

from urllib.parse import urlencode, urlsplit, parse_qs

params = [
    ("q", "fish & chips"),
    ("page", 2),
    ("tag", "python"),
    ("tag", "api"),
    ("in_stock", "true"),
]
url = "https://api.example.com/v1/search?" + urlencode(params, doseq=True)
print(url)
parts = urlsplit(url)
print("round trip:", parse_qs(parts.query))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
https://api.example.com/v1/search?q=fish+%26+chips&page=2&tag=python&tag=api&in_stock=true
round trip: {'q': ['fish & chips'], 'page': ['2'], 'tag': ['python', 'api'], 'in_stock': ['true']}

The two things doing the work are the list of pairs and `doseq=True`. A list of (key, value) pairs — instead of a dict — is what lets the `tag` key legitimately appear twice, and `doseq` tells `urlencode` to emit repeated keys rather than trying to serialize the list itself.

Look at the encoding of the query term: `fish+%26+chips`. The `&` inside the data became `%26`, so the server will decode exactly one `q` parameter whose value is the original string. The round-trip through `parse_qs` proves it: the server side recovers precisely the parameters you meant to send, no more, no fewer.

base_no_slash = "https://api.example.com/v1"
base_slash = "https://api.example.com/v1/"
print("no trailing slash: ", urljoin(base_no_slash, "users"))
print("trailing slash:    ", urljoin(base_slash, "users"))
print("leading slash:     ", urljoin(base_slash, "/users"))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
no trailing slash:  https://api.example.com/users
trailing slash:     https://api.example.com/v1/users
leading slash:      https://api.example.com/users

`urljoin` implements the RFC's relative-resolution rules, and under those rules the last segment of the base is treated as a *file*, not a directory, unless it ends with `/`. So `urljoin("https://api.example.com/v1", "users")` replaces `v1` instead of appending to it — no error, just a quietly wrong URL that 404s somewhere downstream.

The mirror-image trap is the third line: a relative path starting with `/` is resolved from the host root, discarding the whole base path including your version prefix.

In practice: store base URLs with a trailing slash, keep relative paths free of a leading slash, or skip `urljoin` for API work and concatenate a known base with a path you control. The bug is nasty precisely because the result is a well-formed URL — just not the one you wanted.
Which headers should I actually care about when I send an API request? I mostly just set Authorization and hope for the best.

Four earn their place on almost every request:

- `Authorization` — your credential, usually `Bearer <token>` or an API-key scheme the docs specify.
- `Accept: application/json` — declares what you can parse. Without it some APIs default to XML or HTML, and your JSON parser explodes on a response that was never meant for it.
- `Content-Type: application/json` — required whenever you send a body, and it must describe the body you actually sent. Servers commonly ignore or reject a JSON body labeled `text/plain`.
- `User-Agent` — identifies your client. Many APIs throttle or block the default library user-agent, and when you need support, "which client?" is the first question.

Two more worth knowing: header names are case-insensitive (`authorization` and `Authorization` are the same header), so don't debug a casing ghost. And treat headers as data, not decoration — response headers carry pagination links, rate-limit budgets, and `Retry-After`, so the habit of reading them starts on the request side.

Your f-string inserts the value raw, so the quote inside the name terminates the JSON string early and everything after it is garbage — the same concatenation mistake as hand-built URLs, one format over.

`json.dumps` exists precisely to own the escaping rules: quotes, backslashes, newlines, and control characters inside values are escaped according to the JSON spec, every time, including the cases you haven't thought of. The round trip at the end is the proof that matters — the parsed value is byte-for-byte the name you started with.

Rule of thumb: a data structure becomes text exactly once, at the boundary, through the format's serializer. If you ever see JSON, XML, or SQL being assembled with string formatting, that's the bug — if not today, then on the first input that contains the format's punctuation.

name = "quarterly report 2026.pdf"

in a query:   ?name=quarterly+report+2026.pdf
urlencode:    name=quarterly+report+2026.pdf

Both encodings mean "space", but they belong to different parts of the URL. In a query string, `+` is the historical form-encoding for a space, and `quote_plus` / `urlencode` produce it. In a path segment, `+` is just a literal plus sign — a server reading paths will look for a file actually named `quarterly+report+2026.pdf` — so paths need `%20`, which `quote` produces.

The practical rule: `quote` for anything going into the path, `quote_plus` (or just `urlencode`) for anything going into the query. Mixing them up doesn't error; it silently asks for the wrong resource, which makes it a classic "works in my test, 404s in production" bug — test data rarely contains spaces, real file names do.
My POST returns 400 errors even though the JSON looks fine when I print it. A colleague says it might be the Content-Type. How could that matter if the body is correct?

Because the server decides how to interpret — or whether to read — your body based on `Content-Type`, before it ever looks at the bytes. Frameworks route the body to a parser by media type: `application/json` goes to the JSON parser, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` goes to the form parser, and anything unrecognized is often treated as an empty body. Your handler then sees no fields at all and quite correctly reports them missing — a 400 that blames your data when the real fault is the label.

Two adjacent traps: forgetting the header entirely (some clients then default to form encoding and mangle the JSON into a single key), and sending `application/json` without a charset on non-ASCII data — UTF-8 is the JSON default and usually assumed, but stating `application/json; charset=utf-8` removes the ambiguity for stricter servers.

Debugging habit: when a body "looks fine" but the server disagrees, capture the exact request — headers included — and compare against a working request from the API's own examples. The difference is almost never in the JSON you printed; it's in the metadata you didn't.

`parse_qs` drops parameters with empty values by default — `note=` vanishes entirely, so code that checks `"note" in params` concludes the field was never sent. Those are different facts: a callback that sends `note=` is saying "there is no note", while an absent `note` says nothing at all, and handlers that branch on presence will take the wrong path.

Pass `keep_blank_values=True` whenever the distinction matters, which in callback and form data is most of the time. Also note what the output shows about shape: values are always lists (`tag` legitimately holds two), so consuming code must decide per key whether it wants the first value, the only value, or all of them — `parse_qs` will not guess for you.
POST, PUT, PATCH — my team uses POST for every update because it always works. What are we giving up?

Mostly precision, and one safety property.

The conventions: POST creates something new (or triggers an action), PUT replaces a resource completely with the representation you send, PATCH changes only the fields you send. "POST always works" usually means the API tolerates it, not that the meanings are interchangeable.

What you give up:

- **Idempotency.** PUT and PATCH-to-a-state are safe to retry — sending the same replacement twice leaves the same result. POST is not: a retried POST creates a second order, a second charge, a second user. The day your network hiccups mid-request and your retry logic fires, that distinction stops being academic.
- **Intent for intermediaries and tooling.** Caches, gateways, and monitoring all reason from the method. A wall of POSTs is opaque to all of them.
- **Clear contracts.** PUT's "send everything" forces you to know the full state; PATCH's "send the delta" forces the API to define merge behavior. POST-for-everything usually means nobody decided either.

Follow the API's documented methods first — but when you design or choose, know that the method is a promise about retry safety, not just a routing label.
I want to unit-test my API client without any network. How do I structure the code so a test can see exactly what request would have been sent?

Separate *building* the request from *sending* it, and make the sending step a replaceable function. The pattern that works well:

- A `build_request(...)` step that returns a plain description — method, URL, headers, body — as data. Tests assert on that data directly: right path, right query encoding, token present in the header, body is the JSON you meant.
- A `transport` callable with a signature like `transport(method, url, headers, body) -> (status, headers, body)` that the client calls for the actual exchange. Production passes a transport backed by your HTTP library; tests pass a fake that records its arguments and returns canned responses.

This buys you three things. Tests run offline and instantly. The fake's call log is stronger than a mock's expectations — you can assert "exactly one request, and its URL was this". And every cross-cutting behavior you add later (retries, logging, redaction) sits in one place, wrapped around the transport, instead of smeared across call sites.

The smell to avoid is a client that constructs and fires requests inline in every method — that design can only be tested through the network or through heavy monkeypatching, and in practice it just doesn't get tested.
Should identifying info and filters go in the path or the query string? And is there anything that should never go in a URL at all?

Convention: the path names the resource — `/users/42`, `/orders/9182/items` — and the query string qualifies the request: filtering (`?status=open`), sorting (`?sort=-created`), pagination (`?page=3`), search terms. A useful test: path segments answer "which thing", query parameters answer "which view of it". If removing the parameter would name a different resource, it belongs in the path; if it would just show the resource differently, it belongs in the query.

What must never go in a URL, path or query: secrets. URLs are the most-logged string in any system — they land in server access logs, proxy logs, browser history, analytics, error reports, and `Referer` headers sent to third parties. An API key or session token in a query string should be treated as published. Credentials belong in the `Authorization` header, which logging infrastructure is built to treat carefully (and which you should still redact).

Same reasoning, weaker form: keep personal data out of URLs where you can. A URL with an email address in it will be copied into a log file that outlives everyone's intentions.
My filter parameter active=True reaches the API but matches nothing, while the API examples all show lowercase. How do I normalize values before encoding?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
naive:     active=True&archived=False&limit=50&q=None
cleaned:   active=true&archived=false&limit=50

`urlencode` stringifies values with `str()`, and Python's spellings are not the API's spellings: `True` becomes the literal text `True`, and `None` becomes the text `None` — so the naive version asks the server for a parameter `q=None`, a search for the word "None", instead of omitting the parameter.

The cleaning pass encodes three decisions explicitly: booleans become the lowercase literals most APIs expect, `None` means "don't send this parameter at all", and numbers pass through untouched. Doing this in one normalization step — before encoding, in your client wrapper — means every call site gets it right for free. Leaving it to each caller guarantees that one of them ships `active=True` and files a bug against the API.
I check `if status == 200` and treat everything else as "error". How should I actually be reading status codes?

Read them as families, because each hundred-block is a different instruction to you:

- **2xx — it worked**, but check which one: 200 OK, 201 Created (often with a `Location` header for the new resource), 202 Accepted (queued, not done — poll or wait for a callback), 204 No Content (success with an empty body — do not try to parse it).
- **3xx — go look elsewhere.** Redirects carry the real URL in `Location`. Most libraries follow GET redirects automatically but historically not POST ones, and a 307/308 preserves your method and body while a 302 may downgrade a POST to a GET.
- **4xx — your request is wrong** and retrying it unchanged is pointless: 400 malformed, 401 unauthenticated, 403 authenticated but not allowed, 404 no such resource, 409 conflict with current state, 422 semantically invalid, 429 rate-limited (this one *is* retryable — after the delay in `Retry-After`).
- **5xx — the server is wrong**: 500 generic, 502/503 upstream or unavailable, 504 timeout at a gateway. These are the retryable ones, with backoff.

So the handling shape is: branch on the family first, then on the specific code where it changes what you'd do. A single `== 200` check lumps "created", "queued", and "wrong address, here's the right one" into your error path.

The structure mirrors the decision tree: success returns a value, redirect returns the new location as data (following it is the caller's choice), and each failure family raises a *distinct* exception type.

Distinct types are the point. `except NotFound` can fall back to creating the resource, `except AuthError` can trigger a re-login, and `except ServerError` can schedule a retry — three different recoveries that would be impossible if everything collapsed into one generic "API error" carrying a status you have to re-inspect. Note also that 204 flows through the success branch with an empty body: the dispatcher never assumes a payload exists.
My delete call succeeds but then my code crashes parsing the response. The API returns 204. What's happening?

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
A 204 means "success, and there is deliberately no content" — DELETE endpoints use it constantly. Your crash is `json.loads("")`: an empty string is not valid JSON, so the parse throws *after* the operation already succeeded, and depending on where the exception lands, your program may report a successful delete as a failure or even retry it.

The guard is trivial but must be deliberate: check for 204 (or an empty body generally) before parsing, and treat it as a successful `None`. Get in the habit of branching on status first and touching the body second — the body is only meaningful once you know what kind of response you're holding.
An API sometimes omits the discount field and sometimes sends it as null, and my code treats those the same. Show me why they're different and how to handle each.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
{"price": 100} -> no discount info; ask the API / use list price
{"price": 100, "discount": null} -> explicitly no discount
{"price": 100, "discount": 15} -> discount of 15

Absent and null are different statements. Absent means the API didn't tell you — maybe this endpoint doesn't know about discounts, maybe it's an older version. Null means the API looked and the answer is "there is none". Collapsing them with a plain `.get("discount")` (which returns `None` for both) can, for example, make you report "no discount" for a product whose pricing you never actually received.

The sentinel pattern keeps them apart: `dict.get(key, MISSING)` with a unique `object()` as the default can never collide with real data, so the three cases — missing, null, value — each get their own branch. Use it whenever a field is optional in the contract; when a field is *required*, don't default at all — let the missing key raise, because a required field disappearing is a contract break you want to hear about loudly.
My client raises 'HTTP 422' and that's all I ever learn. The API team keeps asking me what the error body said. Why do they care, and what should I do differently?

Because the status code is the headline and the body is the article. A 422 from any maintained API carries a JSON body that names the actual problem — typically an error code, a human message, and often the specific fields that failed validation, like `{"errors": [{"field": "price", "code": "required"}]}`. "HTTP 422" tells you *that* the request was invalid; the body tells you *which part*, which is the difference between a five-minute fix and a guessing session with the API team.

The anti-pattern is calling something like `raise_for_status()` the moment a response arrives: it builds an exception from the status line alone and the body is discarded unread. Instead, on any error status, read and parse the body first, then raise your own exception carrying the status, the API's error code and message, and the request id if one is provided (in the body or a header — support will ask for that too).

Practical rule: an error path that throws away the body is unfinished. Log the parsed error, not just the status, and your future debugging self will notice the difference immediately.

code:   validation_failed
fields: {'price': 'required', 'email': 'invalid format'}

The exception now carries everything the caller needs to act: the status for policy (retry? give up?), the API's own error code for branching, and the field map for showing a user exactly what to fix.

The second case matters just as much: a 502 from a proxy often returns an HTML page, not JSON. The parse attempt fails, the code falls back to a synthesized error with the status in the message, and the caller still gets a clean `ApiError` instead of a `JSONDecodeError` leaking out of the error handler itself. Error paths have error paths — build them so the fallback is boring.
An endpoint moved and the API returns redirects. My GETs follow fine but my POSTs come back as GETs with no body. What's going on?

You're being downgraded by history. The original redirect codes, 301 and 302, were specified ambiguously, and browsers settled on a behavior: when redirecting a POST, reissue it as a GET and drop the body. Most HTTP libraries copy that behavior for compatibility, so your POST arrives at the new address as a bodyless GET — which the endpoint then rejects or, worse, interprets as a list request.

The unambiguous codes exist precisely to fix this: **307** guarantees the method and body are preserved exactly, and **308** is its permanent counterpart. If the API controls the redirect, it should be emitting 307/308 for anything non-GET.

On your side, three defenses: log the final URL and status chain when a request behaves strangely (a silent redirect is invisible otherwise); check whether your library follows redirects for POST at all and what it does with the body; and prefer updating your base URL to the new location over relying on redirects permanently — a redirect is a courtesy for stragglers, not a routing layer, and it costs an extra round trip on every call forever.
I want raise-for-status behavior but only for real errors — redirects and success shouldn't raise. Implement and demonstrate it.

The entire policy is the threshold: below 400, the response is information the caller may want (a redirect target, a 201's location, a 204's quiet success); at 400 and above, it's a failure the caller must not be able to ignore accidentally.

Two refinements worth adding in real clients. First, attach the parsed error body to the exception, as a bare "HTTP 422" wastes the most useful bytes of the response. Second, decide about 429 deliberately: it raises here, which is fine if the catching code knows to read a `Retry-After` value off the exception and back off — what it must not do is fall into a generic "error, give up" bucket.
I parse the JSON body and ignore everything else about a response. What am I missing in the headers?

A second channel of information that several features can't work without:

- **Pagination** — many APIs put the next page in a `Link: <...>; rel="next"` header and totals in `X-Total-Count`. If you only read bodies, you can't page correctly against those APIs at all.
- **Rate limits** — `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`, and on a 429 the all-important `Retry-After`. Reading them lets you slow down *before* you're throttled instead of after.
- **Caching** — `ETag` plus a later `If-None-Match` gets you a cheap 304 Not Modified instead of re-downloading unchanged data; `Cache-Control` tells you how long you may reuse what you have.
- **Debugging** — a request-id header (names vary: `X-Request-Id`, `Request-Id`) is the key support will ask for when you report a problem; log it on errors.
- **Deprecation** — `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers are how APIs warn that an endpoint is scheduled to disappear.

Get in the habit of treating the response as status + headers + body, all three read on purpose. The body is the payload; the headers are the operating instructions.

The correlation with server trouble is the tell. When the API itself is healthy, it answers with JSON. When it's *down*, the thing answering you is often not your API at all — it's a load balancer, proxy, or CDN edge returning its own error page, and those are HTML. Your parser isn't flaky; it's faithfully reporting that a 502 page is not JSON, at the worst possible moment, in the least informative way.

Checking `Content-Type` before parsing turns a confusing `JSONDecodeError` into a correct diagnosis: this was an infrastructure error, retryable, not a data problem. Two supporting habits: branch on status before parsing (a 5xx body needs no parsing at all), and when you log a parse failure, log the first bytes of the body — `<html>` in the log ends the mystery instantly.
An older API I use returns HTTP 200 for everything, even failures. How do I handle that without going mad?

You handle it by adding the check the API skipped: the real status lives inside the body, in an envelope field like `{"ok": false, "error": {"code": "...", "message": "..."}}` or a `status: "error"` member. Your client's response handling becomes two-stage — HTTP status first (still useful: a proxy can 502 even if the API never does), then the envelope's own success flag, and only then the payload.

Wrap this in exactly one place: a single unwrap function that every call passes through, which raises your normal error exception when the envelope says failure, carrying the envelope's code and message. Call sites then see sane behavior and never learn the API's quirk.

What not to do: sprinkle envelope checks through business logic (they'll be forgotten on the next endpoint), or treat "200 but error envelope" as success anywhere. And when you find yourself writing that unwrap function, note the API's error codes carefully — with no HTTP semantics to lean on, those codes are the only signal distinguishing "retry this" from "this will never work", and they are usually documented worse than the endpoints. Log the ones you don't recognize.
An API wraps everything in an envelope with data and meta keys, and errors in an error key. Write the unwrapping logic and show both branches.

arguments.code:
import json

class ApiError(Exception):
    pass

def unwrap(raw):
    env = json.loads(raw)
    if "error" in env and env["error"]:
        raise ApiError(f"{env['error']['code']}: {env['error']['message']}")
    return env["data"], env.get("meta", {})

ok = json.dumps({"data": [{"id": 1}, {"id": 2}],
                 "meta": {"page": 1, "total": 2}})
bad = json.dumps({"error": {"code": "rate_limited",
                             "message": "slow down"}})
bare = json.dumps({"data": {"id": 9}})
data, meta = unwrap(ok)
print("data:", data)
print("meta:", meta)
print("no meta:", unwrap(bare))
try:
    unwrap(bad)
except ApiError as e:
    print("raises ApiError:", e)

data: [{'id': 1}, {'id': 2}]
meta: {'page': 1, 'total': 2}
no meta: ({'id': 9}, {})

Every caller now receives the payload and pagination metadata as a plain pair, and failures arrive as exceptions — the envelope exists only inside this one function.

Details worth copying: the error branch checks the key is present *and* truthy, because some envelope styles include `"error": null` on success; `meta` defaults to an empty dict so callers can always treat it as a dict; and the error message keeps the API's own code, since `rate_limited` is actionable (back off) in a way that a bare "request failed" is not. If you integrate more than one enveloped API, this function — small as it is — is the highest-leverage code you'll write for each of them.
Every API I integrate paginates differently. What are the main styles and how do I recognize which one I'm dealing with?

Three styles cover almost everything:

- **Offset/page pagination** — you send `page`/`offset` and `limit`/`per_page`; responses often include a `total`. Recognize it by numeric parameters and random access: you can ask for page 7 directly.
- **Cursor pagination** — the response hands you an opaque `next_cursor` (or `after` token) and you send it back to get the next chunk; a null or absent cursor means you're done. Recognize it by the token you can't compute yourself. You cannot jump to page 7 — you can only walk.
- **Link-header pagination** — the data is a bare array and the next URL lives in a `Link` response header with `rel="next"`. Recognize it by an array body that seems to have no pagination fields anywhere — they're in the headers.

Recognition procedure for a new API: fetch a deliberately small first page and inspect the *whole* response — body fields and headers — for anything that smells like continuation: `next`, `cursor`, `links`, totals. Then read the docs for that signal only.

The styles are not interchangeable in behavior, either: offset is simple but unstable when data changes mid-walk; cursors are stable and scale; link headers keep bodies clean. Your client code should isolate whichever style behind a single "give me everything" iterator so the rest of the program never finds out which one it was.
Collect all items from an offset-paginated fake API and show me the request pattern and the termination condition.

ITEMS = [{"id": i} for i in range(1, 24)]

def fake_get(offset, limit):
    page = ITEMS[offset:offset + limit]
    return {"items": page, "total": len(ITEMS)}

def collect_all(limit=10):
    collected, offset, requests = [], 0, 0
    while True:
        resp = fake_get(offset, limit)
        requests += 1
        collected.extend(resp["items"])
        if len(collected) >= resp["total"]:
            break
        offset += limit

Why do large APIs prefer cursor pagination over offsets? Offsets seem simpler and let me jump to any page.

Offsets are simpler — for the client. For the server and for correctness, they degrade in two ways.

**Cost.** An offset of 900,000 with a limit of 50 asks the database to produce and discard 900,000 rows to hand you 50. Deep pagination gets slower the further you walk. A cursor encodes "after this specific item" in a stable ordering, which an index can seek to directly — page 10,000 costs like page 1.

**Stability.** Offsets are positions in a changing list: insertions and deletions before your position shift every later window, duplicating or skipping items mid-walk. A cursor names a place in an ordering, so changes elsewhere don't move it.

What you give up is real: random access (no "jump to page 7"), easy parallel fetching of pages, and a visible total. How do I pick a page size? Bigger pages mean fewer requests, so why not always ask for the maximum?

- **Memory and processing spikes.** A page of 10,000 full records must be held and processed as a unit; if your per-item work is slow, you've also delayed the first result by the time it takes to download the whole slab.
- **Failure cost.** A request that dies at item 9,999 of a giant page retries the whole page. Small pages bound the blast radius.

- **Timeouts.** Giant pages take longer to generate server-side; they're the requests most likely to hit a gateway timeout.

The security story follows from that simplicity. Base64 is an *encoding*, not encryption — anyone who sees the header can decode it in one step and recover the password itself, not a token that represents it. So Basic auth is only as safe as the channel: over HTTPS it's a reasonable, if blunt, scheme; over plain HTTP it is broadcasting a reusable password. 2. **API calls.** Send `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` on each request until the token nears expiry, then fetch a new one. There is no refresh token in this grant — when the access token dies, you simply do the token request again with the same credentials.

Implementation points that separate a working integration from a fragile one: cache the token and reuse it until shortly *before* `expires_in` elapses (fetching a token per API call doubles your latency and can trip rate limits on the token endpoint); treat the token endpoint as a dependency that can fail, and retry it with backoff; keep the client secret in the secret store, never in code; and request only the scopes the service actually uses, because the token carries them into every call. What is request signing with HMAC, and when would an API use it instead of just a bearer token?

A bearer token is a secret you *show*; a signature is a secret you *use*. With HMAC signing, the client computes a keyed hash — typically HMAC-SHA256 — over a canonical representation of the request (method, path, body, and usually a timestamp), using the shared secret as the key, and sends the resulting signature in a header. The secret itself never crosses the wire. The server recomputes the signature over what it received and compares: a match proves the request was produced by a holder of the secret *and* that nothing in the signed material was altered in transit.

That buys three properties a bearer token doesn't:

- **Integrity** — a tampered body or path invalidates the signature; a stolen bearer token, by contrast, works from anywhere until it expires.
- **Replay resistance** — when a timestamp (and often a nonce) is part of the signed material and the server rejects old timestamps, a captured request can't simply be resent later.
- **No reusable credential on the wire** — a logged or leaked signature authorizes that one request, not the account.

The costs are real: canonicalization is fiddly (the signature is only valid if both sides serialize identically — a reserialized body or reordered query can break it), clock skew becomes a failure mode, and debugging is harder because you can't just paste the request into a tool and replay it. That's why signing shows up where the stakes justify it — payment APIs, cloud provider APIs, webhook deliveries — and bearer tokens carry the rest.

Retry when the failure is plausibly transient and the request is safe to repeat:

**Retryable:** 429 (rate limited — after the `Retry-After` delay), 500, 502, 503, 504 (server-side, likely temporary), and connection-level failures where the request may never have arrived (DNS hiccups, connection resets, timeouts — with the idempotency caveat below).

**Not retryable as-is:** 400 (your request is malformed; the same bytes will fail identically), 401 (retry only after refreshing the credential, once), 403 (permission won't change), 404 (the thing isn't there), 409 and 422 (the server understood you and said no for a reason that repetition won't change).

**The safety condition:** retrying is only safe if the operation is idempotent — GET, PUT, DELETE by design; POST only with an idempotency key or a server-side dedupe guarantee. A retried non-idempotent POST after a timeout is how duplicate orders and double charges happen: the first attempt may have succeeded and only the *response* was lost.

So the rule composes: status says whether a retry can help, method-plus-key says whether it's safe, and a small attempt budget (commonly 3) plus backoff says how hard to try. Encode all three in your client wrapper once, and no call site ever improvises retry policy again.

Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and what does that actually promise me as a client?

Idempotent means: making the same request N times has the same effect on server state as making it once. The classification:

- **GET** — a read; changes nothing. Safe and idempotent.
- **PUT** — replaces the resource with the representation you send. Sending it twice leaves the same final state as sending it once. Idempotent.
- **DELETE** — removes the resource. The second call may get a 404, but the state (resource absent) is the same. Idempotent in effect.
- **POST** — creates or triggers. N calls, N effects. Not idempotent.
- **PATCH** — it depends: "set price to 50" is idempotent; "add 10 to the count" is not. Read the endpoint's contract.

The promise this buys you is a retry rule you don't have to re-derive per endpoint: idempotent operations can be retried automatically after ambiguous failures (timeouts, resets), because a duplicate delivery is indistinguishable from a single one. How does a circuit breaker fit into an API client? I've only seen the term in architecture diagrams.

A circuit breaker is a failure counter with a memory, wrapped around your calls. It has three states:

- **Closed** (normal): calls pass through. Failures are counted; successes reset the count.
- **Open**: after a threshold of consecutive failures (say 5), the breaker opens and calls *fail immediately, locally*, without touching the network. The struggling server gets silence instead of a continued pounding, and your callers get a fast, predictable error instead of slow timeouts.
- **Half-open**: after a cooldown (say 30 seconds), the breaker lets one trial call through. Success closes the breaker and normal traffic resumes; failure reopens it for another cooldown.

What it buys beyond a retry loop: retries handle *a* transient failure; the breaker handles the *sustained* case, where retrying is actively harmful. - **Timeout:** the most ambiguous of all. The server may still be working on it, or may have finished a millisecond after you gave up. For writes, this is the "unknown state" case.

- **Use the event's own facts.** Events carry the resource's state or a version/sequence from the provider (`created` timestamps on the resource, a monotonically increasing version, the resource's current status). When an event arrives, compare its version against what you have stored: newer wins, older is recorded but doesn't move state backwards.
- **Fetch the truth when it matters.** For consequential transitions, treat the webhook as a doorbell, not the fact itself: on receiving it, fetch the resource's current state from the API and reconcile to that. The doorbell can arrive out of order; the fetched state can't lie about the present.
- **Make states monotonic where the domain allows.** `paid → shipped → delivered` only moves forward; an event that would move state backwards is a stale delivery, and the correct response is to ignore it for state purposes while still acknowledging receipt.

What not to do: process events in arrival order and let the last writer win — that makes your database a function of network timing. And don't buffer-and-reorder with arbitrary delays hoping the "real" order assembles itself; versions and reconciliation solve it deterministically, patience doesn't.

Our webhook endpoint returned 500s during a deploy and now the provider is redelivering thousands of events. What are the dynamics here and how do we calm it down?

You've met the redelivery storm. Providers retry failed deliveries on escalating schedules — minutes, then hours, sometimes for days — and each event that failed during your outage is now on its own retry clock. When you come back up, you don't get the backlog once; you get it as overlapping waves, interleaved with new events, all at-least-once. If your endpoint is still slow, the waves compound: more timeouts, more retries scheduled.

Calming it down, in order:

1. **Make the endpoint cheap and durable.** Its only jobs: verify the signature, write the event to a table or queue, return 2xx. If it does real work inline, fix that first — a fast 2xx stops new retries from being scheduled.
2. **Be idempotent.** The backlog contains duplicates by construction. A receiver that dedupes by event id experiences the storm as noise; one that doesn't experiences it as double charges.
3. **Drain asynchronously at your own pace.** Workers pull from the queue at a rate your downstream systems can handle. The provider's retry schedule stops mattering once the events are safely in *your* storage.
4. **Check the provider's controls.** Many let you pause deliveries, replay from a dashboard, or extend the retry window — better than fighting the schedule.

And afterwards: most providers also stop retrying after a fixed window and mark events as failed-permanently. Reconcile the gap by fetching the affected resources or requesting a replay, because "the storm passed" does not mean "nothing was lost".
I verify webhook signatures, but a security review says I'm still vulnerable to replay attacks. What am I missing?

The signature proves the body is authentic; it says nothing about *when* it was sent. An attacker who captures one genuine signed request — from a log, a proxy, anywhere — can resend it verbatim next week and it will verify perfectly, because the bytes and signature still match. If the event moves money or grants access, you've processed the same fact twice from an untrusted source.

The standard defense is to make freshness part of what's signed: the provider includes a timestamp in the signed material (commonly a header like `t=1699999999` signed together with the body), and the receiver rejects deliveries whose timestamp is too far from now — a tolerance of a few minutes accommodates clock skew and delivery delays. A captured request ages out of the window and becomes worthless.

Two complements: dedupe by event id (you should already) bounds the damage of a replay inside the window, and HTTPS everywhere removes the easiest capture points. When you implement a provider's scheme, follow their exact construction — which fields are signed, in what order, in what encoding — because a verification that ignores the timestamp field while "checking the signature" is precisely the gap your reviewer found.

Our webhook signing secret has been the same for two years and may have been pasted into a ticket once. How do we rotate it without dropping real events?

Treat it as compromised and rotate with overlap, the same shape as API-key rotation:

1. **Generate the new secret in the provider's dashboard.** Most providers support two active secrets during a transition, or let you add a second endpoint configuration. If yours supports only one, plan a short maintenance window and expect to lean on event reconciliation afterward.
2. **Deploy a receiver that accepts both.** Verify against the new secret, and on failure try the old one, logging which one matched. That log is your migration meter.
3. **Watch the old secret go quiet.** Once deliveries verify exclusively against the new secret — across at least one full retry cycle of the provider's schedule, not just an hour — remove the old secret from your receiver and revoke it in the dashboard.
4. **Reconcile the window.** Any events that failed verification during the transition should be replayed from the provider's dashboard or re-fetched via the API; a rotation that silently drops a few events trades a security problem for a data problem.

And fix the process that got you here: the secret belongs in the secret store with access logging, never in tickets, chat, or code. Anyone who has handled it should be able to say where it has been; "pasted into a ticket once" is exactly the sentence that should trigger this procedure.
An API I use has no version in the URL and the provider says they 'improve it continuously'. Last month a field changed type and broke us. How do I protect myself against unversioned drift?

You can't stop the drift, so you build the client to *detect* it early and *absorb* what it safely can:

- **Pin what you can.** Some APIs version via a header (`Accept: application/vnd.api+json; version=2`, or a dated header like Stripe's) even when the URL is bare. If any pinning mechanism exists, use it and record the version you developed against.
- **Parse tolerantly.** Ignore fields you don't know, default optional fields that vanish, and coerce carefully where types wobble (a price that arrives as `"12.50"` or `12.5`). A tolerant reader survives additive and cosmetic change.
- **Validate the contract you depend on.** The fields your code truly needs — presence and type — get checked at the parse boundary, and a violation raises a loud, specific "contract changed" error naming the field. That converts next month's silent corruption into this minute's clear alert.
- **Keep recorded fixtures.** Save real responses and replay them in your test suite; when the provider changes something, your CI against fresh recordings (or a scheduled canary call that validates the live shape) notices before your users do.

And keep the blast radius small: one parsing module owns the API's shape, so when drift happens — it will — the fix lands in one file, not forty call sites.

How do I tell whether an API change is safe for my client or breaking? Providers announce 'non-breaking improvements' that still break me.

Judge by what your client observes, not by the announcement. The reliable taxonomy:

**Safe (additive) changes:** new fields in responses, new optional request parameters, new endpoints, new enum values *if* your code tolerates unknown ones, relaxed validation. A tolerant reader sails through all of these.

**Breaking changes:** a field removed or renamed, a field's type changed (`"5.00"` becoming `5.0` counts), a field that was always present becoming nullable or absent, an enum value removed, an error format changed, pagination or ordering semantics altered, a previously-optional parameter becoming required.

The grey zone is where "non-breaking" announcements go wrong: the provider means "the schema still validates" while your code depended on behavior — the field that was always populated, the list that was always sorted, the enum that only had three values. Those are changes to the *de facto* contract, and no announcement taxonomy covers them.

Your defenses are the ones that don't require trusting announcements: tolerant parsing for the additive side, contract checks on exactly what you depend on, recorded-response tests that diff new behavior against pinned fixtures. If a change can break you, your own checks should be able to catch it — because sooner or later, one will arrive unannounced.

That's an afternoon of work that converts a future outage into a ticket with months of notice.
- **Changelogs and developer newsletters.** Subscribe the team's shared inbox, not an individual's. Deprecations announced to a person who leaves are announcements lost.
- **Your own telemetry.** A sudden change in response shape, new fields appearing, or docs pages moving are soft signals. Contract checks double as deprecation tripwires: the field that becomes nullable today is the field that disappears in the next version.

When you do get notice, the migration is a project, not a patch: find every call site (this is where having one client module pays off), note the sunset date against your release calendar, and run old and new in parallel where the stakes justify it. The teams that get hurt by deprecations are never the ones who couldn't migrate in time — they're the ones who found out from the outage.

What are contract tests for an API client, and how do recorded fixtures fit in? Our integration breaks in production, never in tests.

Your tests pass because they test against your *assumptions* about the API — mocks you wrote, returning what you believe the API returns. Contract testing replaces assumptions with evidence:

- **Record real responses.** During development (or from a sandbox), capture actual responses for the endpoints you use — success bodies, error bodies, headers that matter — sanitized of secrets and personal data, and commit them as fixtures.
- **Test the parser against the fixtures.** Your suite replays recorded responses through your real parsing code. This catches the entire class of "the field is named `total_cents`, not `totalCents`" bugs, because the fixture doesn't care what you believed.
- **Refresh fixtures deliberately.** Periodically re-record from the live API and diff. A changed fixture is a change in the contract, surfaced in a pull request where a human can judge it — instead of in production at random.

If you don't send `Accept`, the server chooses for you — and its default is whatever its framework prefers, which may be XML, may change between versions, and may differ between endpoints of the same API. Clients that omit the header and parse for JSON are betting on a default they don't control.

Handle it as an explicit decision in exactly one place — your client wrapper:

- Send `Accept: application/json` (or the vendor's versioned media type, like `application/vnd.example.v2+json`, which folds format *and* version selection into the one header) on every request.
- On the response side, check the returned `Content-Type` before parsing, and branch or fail clearly if it's not what you asked for. A mismatch means something specific — a proxy error page, a misconfigured endpoint, a version you didn't negotiate — and each deserves its own handling rather than a parser exception.
- If the API offers a format you might migrate to, negotiate deliberately: change the header, watch the contract checks, roll out. Format is a contract term, and like all contract terms it should be set intentionally, verified on receipt, and changed on purpose.
There's no version number anywhere in this API. How do I even reason about compatibility when something changes?

When there's no declared version, the *observed behavior* is the version, and your job is to pin it yourself:

- **Establish a baseline.** Record real responses for every endpoint you use (sanitized fixtures), and write down the behaviors you depend on: field names and types, ordering, pagination semantics, error shapes. That document — even a page long — is your private version number: "we are built against the behavior observed on this date".
- **Detect change against the baseline.** Contract checks at your parse boundary for the fields you depend on, fixture diffs when you re-record, and a scheduled canary call that validates live response shape. Detection converts silent drift into an event you can respond to.
- **Isolate the seam.** One module parses everything the API sends. When behavior changes, the fix is localized and the rest of your program, which speaks in your own types, never hears about it.
- **Feature-detect rather than assume.** Where you need a newer behavior, probe for it (does the response include the field? does the endpoint accept the parameter?) instead of assuming a timeline.

You can't hold an unversioned API to a contract it never signed. What you can do is notice within minutes instead of weeks, and confine the damage to the one module whose entire job is knowing what the API does today.
What should an API client actually log for each request? Our current logs are either nothing or entire payloads with everything in them.

- **Method and path** — with ids in the path is fine; query strings should be redacted or dropped, since they carry tokens and personal data surprisingly often.
- **Status code** and **duration** — the raw material for latency percentiles, error rates, and timeout alarms.
- **The provider's request id** (from the response header or body) — the single most valuable field when you open a support ticket; it's the key to *their* logs.
- **Your correlation id**, if you propagate one, tying this call to the user action or job that caused it.
- **Retry count** and the final outcome, so a request that succeeded on attempt three is visible as such, not as a clean success.

What stays out: request and response bodies (size, secrets, personal data — all three), the `Authorization` header in any form, and API keys even partially beyond a last-four hint if you must distinguish keys. The test for a log line: could you paste it into a ticket with the provider? If yes, it has the right fields and no wrong ones.

- **Default to metadata**: method, path, status, duration, request ids. That answers most debugging questions (which call, when, how did it end).
- **Summarize bodies when you must**: field names and counts, sizes, hashes — shape without content.
- **Redact by construction** for the rare deep-debug capture: a redactor over keys and patterns, applied before anything is written, plus short retention on those specific logs.
- **Make deep capture opt-in and temporary**: a debug flag per request or per tenant, enabled during an investigation and off by default, so the dangerous mode is a deliberate act with an expiry.

The program's interior now works with a `User` — typed fields, defaults applied — and every doubt about the API's shape is resolved in this one function. Required fields are checked for presence, the id's type is verified (with the bool impostor excluded), and the email gets a minimal sanity check, each failure naming the field and the expectation.

Optional fields show the other half of the discipline: `name` and `active` take defaults when absent, because the program can proceed sensibly without them — while `id` and `email` cannot, so their absence is an error, not a default. That per-field decision — required-and-checked versus optional-with-default — *is* your real contract with the API, written in executable form. When the API changes, this function is where the argument happens, and its error messages are the minutes of the meeting.

Every discipline from this batch in one small machine. Auth comes from the environment and is checked by the transport; the first page request eats a 503 and the retry policy — transient statuses only, three attempts — absorbs it invisibly; pagination walks the cursor to null and collects all seven items across three pages; every request is logged with its correlation id and the credential redacted *by construction* (the log statement never touches the real header value); and a 401 would surface as a `PermissionError` naming the environment variable to check, not as a raw status.

None of these pieces is long. The point of the capstone is their composition: because they all live in the client, the calling code is `client.list_all_items()` — one line that inherits correct behavior for auth, failure, scale, and observability. That is the whole argument for building clients this way: correctness that call sites get for free is correctness that actually happens.
